title: Top 5 Customers by Number of Orders
watchOutFor: frequency (order count) ≠ value (revenue, Q03) — different business question, different list.
problem: Operations wants to know which customers order most *frequently* — a different signal than total revenue, useful for spotting high-frequency, potentially lower-basket accounts versus high-value/low-frequency ones.
objective: Identify the 5 customers who placed the highest number of distinct orders.
expectedOutput:
| Column | Description |
|---|---|
| customer_id | Unique identifier of the customer |
| company_name | Customer's company name |
| order_count | Number of distinct orders placed |

| customer_id | company_name | order_count |
|---|---|---|
| SAVEA | Save-a-lot Markets | 31 |
| ERNSH | Ernst Handel | 30 |
| QUICK | QUICK-Stop | 28 |

*(Sample values illustrative of the standard Northwind dataset.)*
approach:
1. Join `customers` to `orders` on `customer_id`.
2. `COUNT(DISTINCT order_id)` per customer.
3. Group by customer.
4. Sort by order count descending.
5. `LIMIT 5`.
mySolution:
SELECT
    cu.customer_id,
    cu.company_name,
    COUNT(DISTINCT o.order_id) AS order_count
FROM customers cu
JOIN orders o ON o.customer_id = cu.customer_id
GROUP BY cu.customer_id, cu.company_name
ORDER BY order_count DESC
LIMIT 5;
solution:
SELECT
    cu.customer_id,
    cu.company_name,
    COUNT(DISTINCT o.order_id) AS order_count
FROM customers cu
JOIN orders o ON o.customer_id = cu.customer_id
GROUP BY cu.customer_id, cu.company_name
ORDER BY order_count DESC
LIMIT 5;
referenceQuery:
SELECT
    cu.customer_id,
    cu.company_name,
    COUNT(DISTINCT o.order_id) AS order_count
FROM customers cu
JOIN orders o ON o.customer_id = cu.customer_id
GROUP BY cu.customer_id, cu.company_name
ORDER BY order_count DESC
LIMIT 5;
why: **Why `COUNT(DISTINCT o.order_id)` rather than `COUNT(o.order_id)`:** with only `customers` joined to `orders` (no `order_details`), each order appears once per customer, so the two are equivalent here. `DISTINCT` is a defensive habit — it prevents inflated counts if the query is later extended to join `order_details`, which duplicates rows per line item.
pitfalls: Joining `order_details` unnecessarily then using plain `COUNT(order_id)` → counts each order once per line item, wildly overstating counts.
Confusing 'most orders' (frequency) with 'most revenue' (value, Q03) — different questions.

followups.question: Why is `COUNT(DISTINCT order_id)` a safer default than plain `COUNT(order_id)`?
followups.answer: With only `customers` joined to `orders`, each order appears once per customer so the two forms are equivalent here. But if the query is later extended to join `order_details` (which has one row per line item), plain `COUNT(order_id)` would count each order once per line item and massively inflate the totals. `COUNT(DISTINCT order_id)` always counts each order exactly once regardless of how the join fans out — a defensive habit that stays correct as the query grows.

followups.question: What's the business difference between a customer here vs the Q03 top-revenue list?
followups.answer: This list ranks by *frequency* (how many orders placed), while Q03 ranks by *value* (total discounted revenue). A high-frequency customer may place many small orders (low basket size), whereas a high-revenue customer may place few large orders. The lists can differ sharply — e.g. SAVEA leads on order count here but QUICK leads on revenue in Q03 — and conflating the two metrics leads to the wrong retention or upsell strategy.

followups.question: How would you extend this to average order count per segment/region?
followups.answer: First aggregate order count per customer (as here), then average those counts grouped by the segment attribute — e.g. wrap this query as a CTE and run `SELECT country, AVG(order_count) FROM per_customer GROUP BY country`, joining back to `customers.country` or `customers.region`. The two-step aggregation (count per customer, then average per segment) avoids mixing grains in a single pass.

followups.question: If you joined `order_details`, what would break and how would you fix it?
followups.answer: `order_details` has one row per line item per order, so joining it multiplies each order's row by its number of line items. A plain `COUNT(o.order_id)` would then count every line item, wildly overstating the order count. The fix is `COUNT(DISTINCT o.order_id)`, which collapses the fanned-out rows back to one per order — exactly why `DISTINCT` is used defensively even when no fan-out exists yet.

takeaway: Separate frequency metrics from value metrics, and use `COUNT(DISTINCT ...)` defensively in joins that may later fan out to a finer grain.
